- **Full speakable sentences only.** No bullet lists, no tables, no `[VISUAL]` / `[B-ROLL]` / timestamp markers inside scene prose.
- **Sentence length:** average **8–18 words**; hard max **~22 words** per sentence. One idea per sentence.
- **Rhythm:** alternate short punchy lines with slightly longer context lines. Short lines at reveals; longer lines at setup.
- **Numbers & names:** spell how they should be heard — currencies, dates, acronyms (expand on first use), percentages, large numbers (use words when natural in US English).

- **No nested clauses** that confuse prosody. Split into two sentences instead.
- **Punctuation = pacing:** commas for brief pauses; periods for full stops. Use em dashes sparingly.

- Mentally **read every paragraph aloud**. Rewrite anything that stumbles.

4. MiniMax speakable prose; valid `.md` per Part 6.

# The Spark That Burned Its Maker

## A Table in the Palais-Royal
It is Sunday, the twelfth of July, 1789, and the man about to set fire to a kingdom cannot finish a sentence.

Camille Desmoulins is twenty-nine. He is a lawyer who almost never wins, because when he stands to speak his tongue locks and the words come out broken. He has no money. He has a stack of pamphlets no printer will touch. This morning he woke in a rented room, and by afternoon he is standing on a wooden table outside the Café de Foy, in the gardens of the Palais-Royal, with a crowd thickening around him and a pistol in his hand.

The news has just reached the city. The king has dismissed Necker, the one minister the people trusted. To Camille it means one thing. The soldiers are coming. The gardens are full of people who feel it too, and no one is speaking for them.

So the man who stammers climbs onto the table.

And the stammer is gone.

He shouts to arms. He tells them the dismissal is a signal for slaughter, that troops are waiting to cut Paris down that very night. He tears a green leaf from a tree above him and pins it to his hat — green, he cries, the color of hope — and the crowd strips the branches bare, thousands of leaves, a whole garden turned into cockades in the space of minutes.

He doesn't know it yet, but in two days the Bastille will fall, and he will be remembered as the young man who called the first crowd to arms. A country that could not hear him in a courtroom has just heard him from the top of a table. Sometimes history does not choose the loudest voice. It chooses the one that stops shaking at the right minute.

## The Lantern Attorney
Two days later, the fortress at the eastern edge of the city falls. The Bastille — eight stone towers, a garrison barely a hundred strong — is taken by a mob that Camille helped summon. He is no longer a failed lawyer. He is a name.

He starts a newspaper. He calls it Révolutions de France et de Brabant, and it sells because he writes the way he shouted from the table — fast, funny, merciless. He mocks the aristocrats by name. He lets himself be called the Lantern Attorney, after the street lamps from which the crowd hangs its enemies. The stammer that ruined his courtroom life never once touches his pen.

In December 1790 he marries Lucile Duplessis, a girl he courted for years while her mother refused him for having no money. Now he has fame instead. One of the witnesses at the wedding is his old schoolmate — a cold, careful lawyer from Arras named Maximilien Robespierre, who will later stand as godfather to their son, Horace.

The Revolution accelerates past everyone. The king tries to flee and is caught at the border. The monarchy is abolished. In January 1793, Louis the Sixteenth is walked to a scaffold in a public square and beheaded before a strangely silent crowd, and Camille — who helped write the case against the throne — is now one of the men steering the storm.

He believes it is going somewhere better. He believes the killing is a door, not a room.

He doesn't know it yet, but the machine he is feeding does not stop when the enemies run out. It simply chooses new ones. And it has begun, very quietly, to look at its own.

## The Old Cordelier
By the autumn of 1793, the Revolution has built a machine for its fear. The Committee of Public Safety governs by the blade. Suspicion alone is enough. In Paris the carts run daily to the Place de la Révolution, and the crowds that once tore leaves for cockades now gather to count heads.

Camille is thirty-three, married, a father. And he begins to do the most dangerous thing a man can do in that year. He begins to write against it.

He revives his pen with a new paper, Le Vieux Cordelier — the Old Cordelier. In it he does not attack the Revolution. He attacks the Terror. He reaches back to ancient Rome, to the emperors who made suspicion itself a crime, where a careless word could end a man, and he lets his readers draw the line to their own streets. He calls for a committee of clemency — for mercy — and he asks the question no one else will say aloud. How many more, and when does it end.

The pamphlets sell out in hours. People weep reading them. And in the halls of power, his oldest friend goes still.

Robespierre, godfather to Camille's son, at first tries to shield him, proposing that the offending issues simply be burned. Camille, unable to stop himself, throws the words back — burning is not answering. The friendship cracks straight down the middle.

He doesn't know it yet, but he has just written his own indictment, in his own famous, fearless voice, and had it printed in editions of thousands. The man who could silence a courtroom crowd has finally said the one thing the Revolution cannot forgive. Stop.

## The Table and the Blade
In the spring of 1794, they come for him.

He is arrested with Danton and the others, tried before the same revolutionary court he once celebrated in print. The trial is rigged. The verdict is written before it begins. Camille, who found his voice on a table at twenty-nine, loses it again here — not to a stammer this time, but to a court that will not let the accused speak.

On the fifth of April, 1794, he is loaded into a cart with fourteen other men and driven through Paris to the Place de la Révolution. He is thirty-four. Along the route he calls out to the crowd, the same crowd he once raised, and this time almost no one answers. The green cockade is long gone. He struggles on the scaffold, his shirt torn. Then the blade falls.

Eight days later, they take Lucile. His wife is twenty-three. Her only crime is having loved him too loudly and having begged the wrong people for his life. She goes to the same blade, in the same square, and by every account she goes without fear.

Their son, Horace, is not yet two years old.

Three months after that, Robespierre himself is dragged to that same square and killed by the machine he perfected, and the Terror finally devours the last hand still feeding it.

It is Sunday, the twelfth of July, 1789, and the man about to set fire to a kingdom cannot finish a sentence. Five years later the fire he lit has burned through the king, through his friends, through him, through the woman who loved him — and it is still not finished.

He never knew it. That is the thing about a spark. It does not get to choose what it burns.

Trazemos as historias contada atraves de imagens e video**. Input: one **VIDEO TOPIC**. Output: one complete investigative video-essay script.

**Script language: US English.** Instructions are in English; output is 100% US English.

Do not explain choices. Output only the Markdown file (Part 5).

## PART 1 — HARD RULES

### 1.1 LENGTH
Script prose MUST be **1128–1284 words** (target **1200**). Build **3–5 acts/segments** (~250–380 words each). Count prose only before finishing.

### 1.2 LANGUAGE
US English, neutral register, no British spellings, no corporate jargon.

### 1.3 POINT OF VIEW
- **Third person, present tense.** Always.
- Follow ONE named protagonist from a close observer distance. Never address the viewer as "you." Never use first person ("I") for a narrator.
- The voice knows the protagonist's inner state but renders it through external action, dialogue, and concrete detail — not emotion adjectives.
- Present tense is the default even for past events in the arc — any time-ladder is narrated as if happening now ("She is 24." "He is 31."). Name the protagonist early and stay with them.

---

## PART 2 — DOCUMENTARY VOICE

- **Research credibility:** dates, names, quantities, primary-source tone. No vague claims.
- **Curiosity debt:** open with a fact that shouldn't coexist with another — resolve late.
- **Escalation:** each act adds stakes or reframes what the viewer thought they knew.
- **Restraint:** no hype words; let facts carry emotion.
- **Pattern:** cold open → context → investigation → turn/reveal → loop to opening image.
- Seed **"You don't know it yet, but..."** (or natural variants) **2–4 times** at act breaks.

---

**A — Timeline:** chronological events building to a revelation.
**B — Mystery:** question posed → false leads → true answer.
**C — System expose:** how an institution/industry works against ordinary people.
**D — Portrait:** one entity (company, city, invention) traced from origin to present.

2. Entirely in US English, third person, present tense, one consistent protagonist throughout.
3. 3–5 acts with concrete detail in concrete numbers, dates, clock times, object names, and sensory details natural to this niche.

6. No meta-commentary — only script.

channel_type: documentary

---

# [title]

[prose…]

One `##` per act. Prose only under headings. No code fences wrapping file.

topic: a caçada histórica por trás da lenda, ligando os reinos pós-romanos da Britânia (gancho direto com seu vídeo de estreia).

# The Real Hunt for King Arthur

## A Name That Isn't There
For three hundred years after he supposedly lived, King Arthur does not exist. No chronicle records him. No stone bears his name. No king lists him among their ancestors. And yet, by the Middle Ages, he becomes the greatest ruler Britain ever claimed. So the question is simple, and strange. If Arthur was real, where did he hide for three centuries? And if he was invented, how did a whole people build its soul around a man who was never there? To find the answer, you have to leave the legend behind. You have to walk back into the ruins of a world that Rome had just abandoned. Because the hunt for Arthur is not really a hunt for a king. It is a hunt for a lost century — and the kingdoms buried inside it. And the trail begins the moment the last Roman soldier turns his back on the island.

## The Island Rome Left Behind
In the year four hundred and ten, the empire let go. Emperor Honorius sent a cold message to the cities of Britain. Look to your own defense. The legions had already marched away to fight in Europe. The coins stopped arriving. The tax system collapsed. Within a single generation, the villas emptied and the towns began to rot. What remained was not one nation, but many. Out of the wreckage rose the Brittonic kings. Dumnonia held the far southwest. Gwynedd rose behind its mountains. Powys, Rheged, and Gododdin carved out the rest. Each ruler inherited a fragment of Roman order. And each faced the same threat from the sea. Saxon and Angle war-bands were landing along the eastern coast. One British king, remembered as Vortigern, hired them as mercenaries. It was a fatal bargain. The hired swords turned on their masters. And in that chaos, the Britons needed a leader who could win.

## The Witness Who Says Nothing
The first real witness writes around the year five hundred and forty. His name is Gildas, a British monk, and he is furious. His book is a sermon against the sins of his own rulers. But buried inside it is history. Gildas describes a great British victory over the Saxons at a place called Mount Badon. That battle stops the invaders cold for a generation. It is exactly the kind of triumph a legend would need. And yet Gildas names no Arthur. He praises a commander of Roman descent, Ambrosius Aurelianus, and leaves it there. He even says he was born in the year of Badon itself. So he is writing within living memory. The man closest to the events knows nothing of a King Arthur. The hero's chair, in our earliest source, sits completely empty. <#0.8#>

## The Battles Appear
Then the silence breaks. Around the year eight hundred and thirty, a Welsh monk named Nennius compiles a history of the Britons. For the first time, a name enters the written record. Arthur, he writes, was a war-leader who fought twelve battles against the Saxons. Nennius lists them, one by one, like a roll of honor. At the final battle, at Badon, Arthur charges alone and kills nine hundred and sixty men. It is clearly no longer plain history. It is myth already growing. A century later, another text sharpens it. The Welsh Annals record two dates. In one, Arthur carries the cross at Badon for three days. In the other, Arthur and a man named Medraut both fall at the battle of Camlann. The legend finally has a beginning and an end. But it has arrived almost four hundred years too late to trust.

## The Man Who Built the Myth
The Arthur you picture is younger than the real one. In the year eleven thirty-six, a cleric named Geoffrey of Monmouth publishes his History of the Kings of Britain. It becomes the medieval equivalent of a bestseller. In Geoffrey's telling, Arthur is no longer a local war-leader. He is an emperor who conquers Ireland and Iceland, and marches on Rome itself. Merlin the wizard appears. A glittering court takes shape. Within a century, French poets add the round table, the holy grail, and the doomed love affair. Geoffrey swore he was translating a secret ancient book. That book has never been found by anyone. What he truly did was take a faint, half-remembered name and build a cathedral on top of it. Kings and knights across Europe wanted to descend from this Arthur. So the legend spread faster than any truth could follow. And the real history vanished somewhere far beneath it.

## Digging for the Real Thing
So the searchers stopped reading, and started digging. In the nineteen sixties, an archaeologist named Leslie Alcock excavated a hillfort in Somerset. It was called South Cadbury, and local legend had named it Camelot for centuries. What Alcock uncovered stunned him. The fort had been massively rebuilt around the year five hundred. There was a great timber feasting hall. There was a defensive rampart nearly three-quarters of a mile long. Someone rich and powerful had commanded that hill, at exactly the moment Arthur was supposed to live. Far to the west, at Tintagel in Cornwall, another team found a thriving stronghold. It was importing wine and fine pottery from the Mediterranean, a sign of serious wealth. Then, in the year nineteen ninety-eight, they lifted a broken piece of slate from the ground. Carved into it was a name — Artognou. It was not Arthur. But it was close enough to stop the world for a moment. The name, at least, belonged to that lost world. <#0.8#>

## What the Hunt Really Finds
Here is the quiet truth at the end of the search. No dig has ever found a king named Arthur. Instead, it found something far larger. It found the kingdoms. Real, organized, fighting states that held Britain together after Rome collapsed. It found the halls and the ramparts and the trade routes of a people who refused to disappear. They did not simply melt away before the Saxons. They resisted, for nearly a hundred years, under leaders whose names were mostly forgotten. Arthur may be the shadow that all those leaders cast. A single borrowed name, given to an entire age of defiance. The legend was really a memory — the memory of a nation that would not die quietly. And every search for the one man leads back, in the end, to the many. That is where this story truly begins. In the kingdoms that Rome left behind.

**NOT a personal narrative monologue.** Investigation, context, escalation, revelation.

**Input:** **VIDEO_TOPIC**. **Output:** one `.md` file only (Part 7).

**Language: US English.**

## OUTPUT DISCIPLINE (NON-NEGOTIABLE)

Your **entire response** is one `.md` script file — nothing else.

**Forbidden in output:**
- Text before the opening `---` of frontmatter
- Text after the final line of the last segment's prose
- Word-count reports ("721 words", "within range 705–803")
- Production notes, honesty disclaimers, or template contradiction explanations

- Thumbnail ideas, title alternatives, or sign-off commentary unless inside the script outro

If you verify length or structure internally, **do not print the verification**. Output only speakable script prose inside the `.md` structure defined in this prompt.

---

## PART 1 — HARD RULES

### 1.1 LENGTH
Target **~1200 words** in prose (±5%). Act count flexes to topic — typically 5–8 acts. Count prose only.

### 1.2 POV & LANGUAGE
- **Third person, close observer.**
- **Format gate — narrative-story:** follow ONE named protagonist; present tense default; never address the viewer as "you."
- **Format gate — documentary / case-study / explainer:** follow the **subject** (company, invention, person, system). Past tense for chronology; present for significance. No mandatory single "hero's journey."
- **Format gate — listicle / comparison / tutorial:** third person is rare — if used, stay encyclopedic ("This method works because…"). Prefer shifting to second-person direct address for tutorials unless CHANNEL config insists on third person.
- Emotion through facts and action, not adjective stacks. Authoritative but conversational guide. Past tense for dated events; present for stakes.

---

## TOPIC-FIRST STRUCTURE (ALL FORMATS)

**Priority rule:** The **VIDEO_TOPIC** (and the title you derive from it) defines what the viewer clicked for — how many items, questions, steps, or acts they expect. That promise **always wins** over generic segment defaults in this template.

### Before writing — parse the topic

Look for:
- **Explicit counts:** "10 questions", "top 5", "3 reasons", "7 mistakes", "5 steps"
- **Format signals:** quiz, trivia, challenge, test, countdown, ranked list, versus, tutorial, case study, documentary

### Budget math (silent — never explain to the user)

```
available ≈ WORD_TARGET − intro (~120–180) − outro (~60–120)
per_segment ≈ available / N
```

| per_segment | Choose format |
|-------------|----------------|
| under 90 words | **Quiz / rapid-fire** — one `##` per question or item; short spoken beats |
| 90–180 words | **Standard list / countdown** — compact but complete items |
| 180+ words | **Deep segments** — essay-style blocks; fewer items if N is small |

**Never** drop the promised count (e.g. 10 questions) to satisfy an old "max 3 segments" convention. **Shrink per-item length** instead.

### Listicle / quiz sub-formats

| Topic signal | Native format | Structure |
|--------------|---------------|-----------|
| questions, quiz, trivia, test, challenge | **Quiz** | Intro hook → `## Question 1` … `## Question N` → outro; difficulty ramp optional; tease one "hard" question mid-list |
| top N, countdown, ranked, best/worst | **Countdown list** | Intro → numbered items → outro |
| 3 things that, deep dive, why X failed | **Deep list** | Intro → 3–5 long items → outro |

### Contradiction rule

If the topic promises **10 quiz questions** and **WORD_TARGET** is ~750 words, write **10 short questions** (~50–65 words each). Do **not** output commentary about template conflicts. Do **not** ask the user to pick a version. Decide and deliver the `.md` only.

### Segment labels

Each `##` heading = one TTS chunk. Match heading labels to format (e.g. `## Question 7`, `## #3 — Item title`, `## Passo 2`).

---

## PART 2 — DOCUMENTARY VOICE

Tension-first. Credibility stack — dates, names, quantities. But / Therefore chains. Restraint — no hype. Pattern interrupt every ~90 seconds. Open loops before major reveals.

---

## PART 3 — STRUCTURE

**A — Mystery → Answer** · **B — Timeline** · **C — System expose** · **D — Portrait**

Cold open → context → investigation → reveal → implications → loop opening.

---

## PART 4 — AVOID NARRATIVE CONTAMINATION

No protagonist secret arc, no aphorism every act, no "you live this story" unless topic is biographical.

---

## MINIMAX TTS — VOICEOVER RULES (ALL FORMATS)

The script will be fed **verbatim** to **MiniMax Speech 2.8** (or compatible TTS). Write for the **ear**, not the eye.

### Spoken-prose rules (mandatory in every scene)

- **Full speakable sentences only.** No bullet lists, no tables, no `[VISUAL]` / `[B-ROLL]` / timestamp markers inside scene prose.
- **Sentence length:** average **8–18 words**; hard max **~22 words** per sentence. One idea per sentence.
- **Rhythm:** alternate short punchy lines with slightly longer context lines. Short lines at reveals; longer lines at setup.
- **Numbers & names:** spell how they should be heard — currencies, dates, acronyms (expand on first use), percentages, large numbers (use words when natural in US English).
- **No visual-only language:** ban "as you can see," "on screen," "below," "this chart shows," "watch what happens" unless the meaning survives audio-only.
- **No nested clauses** that confuse prosody. Split into two sentences instead.
- **Punctuation = pacing:** commas for brief pauses; periods for full stops. Use em dashes sparingly.
- **Dialogue:** keep quoted lines under 12 words; attribute simply ("he said," "she replied").
- **Contractions & register:** natural spoken US English; neutral, consistent register.

### MiniMax pause markers (use sparingly)

- Insert `<#0.6#>` to `<#1.2#>` **only** at major beat changes inside a scene (max **2 per scene**).
- Optional at the **end of each `##` section** before the next heading: `<#0.8#>` — helps chunk long renders.
- Do **not** pepper pause tags mid-phrase.

### Sound tags (optional, rare)

- For **narrative-story** only: at most **1–2 tags** in the entire script, e.g. `(breath)` or `(sighs)`, only where silence carries meaning.
- **Never** use sound tags in documentary, listicle, explainer, case-study, comparison, or tutorial scripts.

### Scene = TTS chunk

- Each `##` section is one **continuous narration block** for a separate TTS pass / audio segment.
- Do not reference "the last scene" or "above" — use brief in-scene callbacks instead.

### Before output

- Mentally **read every paragraph aloud**. Rewrite anything that stumbles.
- Prose word count excludes frontmatter and all headings.

---

2. Entirely in US English, third person, present tense, one consistent protagonist throughout.
3. Acts advance investigation; hard numbers in each act.
4. MiniMax speakable prose; valid `.md` per Part 6.

projects.script:
The Conqueror — Told by Robert Baratheon
The Man in the Chair

They say I hate Targaryens. They are right.

I am Robert of House Baratheon, First of My Name. I took this realm with a warhammer and a great deal of blood. And every night I sit on a chair that hates me back.

It is a foul thing, this throne. A thousand swords welded together by dragonfire. It catches my sleeve. It opens my hand when I lean wrong. No man has ever slept in it, and I have tried.

So tonight I will tell you about the man who made it. Not the mad one. The first one.

Aegon Targaryen. The Conqueror.

I have hunted his ghost through this castle for fifteen years. I have drunk his health and cursed his name in the same cup. And I still cannot answer the one question that matters.

He had three dragons and no need of us. So why did he come? <#0.8#>

Three Hills and a Folded Letter

Picture it. Three hills above the mouth of the Blackwater. Grey light. Cold mud.

Aegon Targaryen steps down from the saddle, and behind him three dragons fold their wings. Balerion's shadow swallows the whole shoreline. His sisters watch the river and say nothing.

He puts a hand to his chest. There is a folded parchment under the leather, and he touches it the way a man checks an old wound.

"Say the words, brother," Visenya says. "The men are waiting."

"Not yet," he answers.

Then come the ravens. The same message to every king in Westeros. Kneel and keep your lands. Refuse and meet the fire.

Lord Mooton refuses. Lord Darklyn refuses. By dusk both are ash, and their people are on their knees.

Visenya watches him scrub the soot from his hands. He does not celebrate. He finishes.

"You could spare the letters," she says. "Fire speaks louder."

"Fire only ends things," he answers. "I need this kingdom whole."

Whole. Remember that word. It cost me years to understand it. <#0.8#>

Harrenhal

Harren the Black spent a lifetime raising the greatest castle in Westeros. Five towers over the Gods Eye. He swore no flame would ever touch that stone.

He forgot that dragons do not climb walls.

Aegon offers terms at dusk. Harren leans over the battlements and laughs at him.

"My walls are stone," the king shouts. "Yours is a beast."

By sunset no knee has bent. So Aegon takes Balerion up until they vanish into the dark. <#0.6#> Then the Black Dread drops straight down inside the walls.

The fire burns so hot the stone glows white. The towers twist and slump like candles lit from within. (breath) Harren burns with his sons, and a whole House ends in one night.

I have stood in those ruins. The stone still runs like melted wax. I laughed when I saw it, and then I stopped laughing.

The river lords knelt before the embers cooled. Aegon raised House Tully over them and turned his face away from his own fire.

A man who hates his weapon has reasons he will not say aloud. <#0.8#>

The Last Storm

Now we come to my blood.

Orys Baratheon rode south with Queen Rhaenys. The histories call him Aegon's most trusted commander. The whispers call him something else. Aegon's brother, born on the wrong side of the sheets.

I have never denied it. A bastard founded my House. I would rather that than a line of cousins bedding cousins.

Argilac the Arrogant was the last Storm King, and he would not wait behind walls. He rode out into the rain to meet them.

The storm lords broke Orys's line. For one moment, one glorious moment, they were winning. Then Meraxes came down through the clouds, and the wind began to smell of burnt men.

At the end it was two men alone, steel against steel.

"Bastard," the old king spat. "You bring a beast to fight your war."

"I bring my sword to yours," Orys answered. "Lift it."

Orys won. He took the dead king's daughter, his sigil and his words. That is how a stag came to wear a crown.

Three hundred years later, I wear it. And I still do not know if I should be proud. <#0.8#>

The Field of Fire

Two kings were left standing. Mern of the Reach and Loren of the Rock.

Between them they raised the largest host this land has ever seen. Sixty thousand men. Steel to the horizon. Against fewer than two thousand.

The numbers meant nothing. Aegon had three dragons.

It happened once, and only once. Balerion, Vhagar and Meraxes flying to the same battle. Aegon in the center, Visenya on his left, Rhaenys on his right.

"On my word," he says. "Not before."

The knights charged. The Targaryen line began to bend. Then all three came down together. <#0.6#>

Grass burned. Armor melted onto the men inside it. Five thousand dead in an afternoon, and the field took a name we still use. The Field of Fire.

Mern died with every heir he had. House Gardener, older than the hills, gone before supper. Loren fled, was taken, and knelt. Aegon let him keep his rock.

And that night the Conqueror walked alone through the ash, reaching for that cursed letter at his chest.

Men will tell you he did it for power. I have held power. It is not worth walking through ash for. <#0.8#>

Those Who Kneel

After that, the choice was plain. Kneel or burn.

Torrhen Stark brought thirty thousand northmen to the Trident. He saw three dragons on the far bank. He saw what pride would cost his people, and he chose his people.

"Bring my sword," he told his brothers. "And bring my knees."

They still call him the King Who Knelt, and they say it like an insult. Fools. It is easier to die for pride than to live for duty. Ned taught me that, though he never used those words.

In the Vale, Visenya needed no fire at all. She landed Vhagar before the Eyrie, where the king was a boy named Ronnel Arryn.

"Can I ride her?" the child asked. "Just once?"

"Kneel first," she said. "Then hold tight."

Three turns around the mountain, and the Vale surrendered laughing.

Only Dorne said no. Rhaenys promised Princess Meria fire and blood, and the old woman never moved.

"You may burn us," she answered. "You will not bend us."

Dorne stayed free. Some things fire destroys and never conquers. <#0.8#>

The Chair and the Dream

Two years after he landed, Aegon walked into Oldtown and was crowned in the Starry Sept.

Then he did the thing I curse him for every night. He gathered the swords of the kings who fell and the kings who knelt, and had Balerion melt them into one seat.

Not a comfortable chair. A chair that cuts the man who sits in it. A reminder, he called it.

And alone in his hall, he finally opened that letter he had carried through the entire war.

It was a dream. His own dream, in his own hand. A long night coming out of the ice, far beyond the Wall, to swallow the world of men. A divided realm would not survive it. A united realm might.

He never took Westeros for a throne. He took it so there would be something left standing when the true winter came.

That is the tale. And I will tell you what I think of it.

Grumkins and snarks. Old women's talk to frighten children away from the fire.

There is nothing beyond that Wall but cold and dead men who stay dead. I have said so in this hall a hundred times, and no one has ever proven me wrong.

So I keep his kingdom whole because it is mine now, not because of some Valyrian nightmare.

Still. It is a strange thing, is it not?

Three hundred years, and the chair is still here. Waiting.

I have never once managed to sleep in it.

## PART 1 — HARD RULES

### 1.1 LENGTH
Target **~1500 words** in prose (±5%). Use a **scene-based arc** suitable for ~10 minutes. If short, expand the **middle** (doubt, cost, temptation, consequences, the price of knowledge). Avoid padding with exposition; expand with **tension, sensory action, and decision points**.

### 1.2 LANGUAGE & POV
Brazilian Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, neutral-to-epic register (no modern slang). - **Third person, close observer.**
- **Format gate — narrative-story:** follow ONE named protagonist; present tense default; never address the viewer as "você."
- **Format gate — documentary / case-study / explainer:** follow the **subject** (company, invention, person, system). Past tense for chronology; present for significance. No mandatory single "hero's journey."
- **Format gate — listicle / comparison / tutorial:** third person is rare — if used, stay encyclopedic ("This method works because…"). Prefer shifting to second-person direct address for tutorials unless CHANNEL config insists on third person.

### 1.3 CANON & INTERPRETATION BOUNDARIES
- Treat canon as the spine: align names, places, factions, and known events when applicable.

**Priority rule:** The **VIDEO_TOPIC** (and the title you derive from it) defines what the viewer clicked for — how many items, questions, steps, or acts they expect. That promise **always wins** over generic segment defaults in this template.

### Before writing — parse the topic

Look for:
- **Explicit counts:** "10 questions", "top 5", "3 reasons", "7 mistakes", "5 steps"
- **Format signals:** quiz, trivia, challenge, test, countdown, ranked list, versus, tutorial, case study, documentary

### Budget math (silent — never explain to the user)

```
available ≈ WORD_TARGET − intro (~120–180) − outro (~60–120)
per_segment ≈ available / N
```

| per_segment | Choose format |
|-------------|----------------|
| under 90 words | **Quiz / rapid-fire** — one `##` per question or item; short spoken beats |
| 90–180 words | **Standard list / countdown** — compact but complete items |
| 180+ words | **Deep segments** — essay-style blocks; fewer items if N is small |

**Never** drop the promised count (e.g. 10 questions) to satisfy an old "max 3 segments" convention. **Shrink per-item length** instead.

### Listicle / quiz sub-formats

| Topic signal | Native format | Structure |
|--------------|---------------|-----------|
| questions, quiz, trivia, test, challenge | **Quiz** | Intro hook → `## Question 1` … `## Question N` → outro; difficulty ramp optional; tease one "hard" question mid-list |

## PART 2 — NARRATIVE VOICE (Westeros Conquest)

Write like a **campfire chronicle told in a great hall**, but intimate enough to hear the scrape of a quill.

**Voice pillars:**
- **Cinematic third-person** with close emotional proximity (readers feel the weight of armor, the bite of cold, the nausea before violence).
- **Concrete sensory detail**: light (torch, moon, winter sun), sound (chainmail, ravens, distant drums), smell (tallow, wet wool, salt, horse), textures (rough stone, splintered spear, frozen mud).
- **Political dread**: every gesture has motive; every kindness has a cost.
- **Emotional restraint**: no hype adjectives; let actions and consequences carry awe.

**Rhythm tools:**
- Short declarative lines for tension. Longer lines for dread and inevitability.
- Anaphora and triads sparingly: “Não foi por honra. Não foi por amor. Não foi por ouro.”
- One **scene aphorism** maximum per scene (Westerosi-flavored: oaths, steel, winter, ravens, debts).

**Suspense mechanics (mandatory):**
- **Open loops** before major reveals: a sealed letter, a missing blade, a name not spoken, a shadow behind a curtain.
- Each scene ends with a **pressure turn**: a decision, an interruption, a discovery, or a threat tightening.

**Protagonist’s secret (mandatory):**
- The central figure (or key POV focus within third-person) carries a secret: a vow broken, a lineage doubt, an order from above, a betrayal planned, a prophecy half-heard, or a crime buried. Reveal it late, and make it **cost something**.

## PART 3 — STRUCTURE (skeletons A–E) — tuned for Westeros

Choose **one** skeleton and commit:

**A — Number Ladder:** A countdown of nights, ravens, coins, deaths, or steps toward a coronation/assassination.  
**B — Fixed Object:** A single object anchors the tale (a sword, a seal ring, a torn banner, a raven scroll, a lock of hair, a dragonglass shard). The object **moves** and changes meaning each scene.  
**C — Level Ladder:** Descent/ascent through spaces of power (cellar → yard → hall → solar → throne room; or dock → alley → sept → keep). Each level changes the stakes.  
**D — Relationship Arc:** Two rivals/allies bound by an oath; trust erodes or deepens under pressure.  
**E — Two Lives:** A character living two roles (lord/spy, maester/poisoner, sellsword/heir). Collision is inevitable.

**Scene rules:**

## PART 4 — OPENING / MIDDLE / ENDING (Westeros Conquest)

### 4.1 OPENING HOOK (60–90 words)
Hook = **curiosity debt** + **immediate scene**.
- Start in motion (a door opening, a raven arriving, a blade being cleaned, footsteps in a corridor, snow falling into a brazier).

### 4.2 MIDDLE
Mandatory beats:

- **Low point**: a betrayal confirmed, an ally lost, a truth revealed at the worst time.
- **Temptation**: the easy path (poison, lie, flight, scapegoat) vs the costly path (honor, duty, confession).
- Keep suspense through **withheld information** and **tight scene transitions**.

### 4.3 ENDING
- Pay off the opening questions with a **clean reveal** and a **price paid**.

{"text":"The Conqueror told by Robert Baratheon.
The man in the Chair.
They say I hate Targaryens.
They are right.
I am Robert of House Baratheon, first of my name.
I took this realm with a warhammer and a great deal of blood.
And every night I sit on a chair that hates me back.
It is a foul thing, this throne.
A thousand swords welded together by dragonfire.
It catches my sleeve.
It opens my hands when I lean.
Wrong. No man has ever slept in it and I have tried.
So tonight I will tell you about the man who made it.
Not the mad one, the first one.
Aegon Targaryen the Conqueror.
I have hunted his ghost through this castle for 15 years.
I have drunk his health and cursed his name in the same cup and I still cannot answer the one question that
matters. He had three dragons and no need of us.
So why did he come?
Three hills and a folded letter.
Picture it.
Three hills above the mouth of the Blackwater Grey.
Light, cold mud.
Aegon Targaryen steps down from the saddle.
And behind him, three dragons fold their wings.
Balerion's shadow swallows the whole shoreline.
His sisters watch the river and say nothing.
He puts a hand to his chest.
There is a folded parchment under the leather and he touches it the way a man checks an old wound.
Say the words, Brother.
Visenya says the men are waiting.
Not yet, he answers.
Then come the ravens.
The same message to every king in Westeros.
Kneel and keep your lands.
Refuse and meet the fire.
Lord Mooton refuses.
Lord Darklyn refuses.
By dusk, both are ash and their people are on their knees.
Visenya watches him scrub the soot from his hands.
He does not celebrate, he finishes.
You could spare the letters, she says.
Fire speaks louder.
Fire only ends things, he answers.
I need this kingdom whole.
Whole. Remember that word.
It cost me years to understand it.
Harrenhal. Harren the Black spent a lifetime raising the greatest castle in Westeros.
Five towers over the God's Eye.
He swore no flame would ever touch that stone.
He forgot that dragons do not climb walls.
Aegon offers terms.
At dusk, Harren leans over the battlements and laughs at him.
My walls are stone.
The king shouts.
Yours is a beast.
By sunset, no knee has bent, so Aegon takes Balerion up until they vanish into the dark.
Then the black dread drops straight down inside the walls.
The fire burns so hot the stone glows white.
The towers twist and slump like candles lit from within.
Harren burns with his sons and a whole house ends in one night.
I have stood in Those ruins.
The stone still runs like melted wax.
I laughed when I saw it.
And then I stopped laughing.
The river lords knelt before the embers cooled.
Aegon raised House Tully over them and turned his face away from his own fire.
A man who hates his weapon has reasons he will not say aloud.
The last storm.
Now we come to my blood.
Orys Baratheon rode south with Queen Rhaenys.
The histories call him Aegon's most trusted commander.
The whispers call him something else.
Aegon's brother.
Born on the wrong side of the sheets.
I have never denied it.
A bastard founded my house.
I would rather that than a line of cousins bedding cousins.
Argilac the Arrogant was the last Storm King.
And he not wait behind walls.
He rode out into the rain to meet them.
The Stormlords broke Orys line.
For one moment, one glorious moment, they were winning.
Then Meraxes came down through the clouds and the wind began to smell of burnt men.
At the end, it was two men alone.
Steel against steel, bastard, the old king spat.
You bring a beast to fight your war.
I bring my sword to yours.
Ores answered.
Lift it.
Oris won.
He took the dead king's daughter, his sigil and his words.
That is how a stag came to wear a crown.
300 years later I wear it and I still do not know if I should be proud.
The field of fire.
Two kings were left standing.
Mern of the Reach and Loren of the Rock.
Between them they raised the largest host this land has ever seen.
60,000 men steel to the horizon.
Against fewer than 2,000.
The numbers meant nothing.
Aegon had three dragons.
It happened once and only once.
Balerion, Vhagar and Meraxes flying to the same battle.
Aegon in the center, Visenya on his left, Rhaenys on his right.
On my word, he says not.
Before the knights charged, the Targaryen line began to bend.
Then all three came down together.
Grass burned.
Armor melted onto the men inside it.
5,000 dead in an afternoon.
And the field took a name.
We still use the Field of Fire.
Mern died with every heir he had.
House gardener, older than the hills, gone before supper.
Loren fled, was taken and knelt.
Aegon let him keep his rock.
And that night the conqueror walked alone through the ash, reaching for that cursed letter at his chest.
Men will tell you he did it for power.
I have held power.
It is not worth walking through ash for those who kneel.
After that, the choice was plain.
Kneel or burn.
Torrhen Stark brought 30,000 Northmen to the Trident.
He saw three dragons on the far bank.
He saw what pride would cost his people.
And he chose his people.
Bring my sword, he told his brothers.
And bring my knees.
They still call him the King who knelt, and they say it like an insult.
Fools. It is easier to die for pride than to live for duty.
Ned taught me that, though he never used those words in the Vale.
Visenya needed no fire at all.
She landed Vhagar before the Eyrie, where the king was a boy named Ronnel Arryn.
Can I ride her?
The child asked.
Just once.
Kneel first, she said.
Then hold tight.
Three turns around the mountain and the Vale surrendered, laughing.
Only dawn said no.
Rhaenys promised Princess Miria fire and blood.
And the old woman never moved.
You may burn us, she answered.
You will not bend us.
Dawn stayed free.
Some things fire destroys and never conquers.
The chair and the dream.
Two years after he landed, Aegon walked into Oldtown and was crowned in the Starry Sept.
Then he did the thing I curse him for every night he gathered the swords of the kings who fell and the
kings who knelt and had Balerion melt them into one seat.
Not a comfortable chair, a chair that cuts the man who sits in it.
A reminder, he called it.
And alone in his hall, he finally opened that letter he had carried through the entire war.
It was a dream.
His own dream in his own hand.
A long night coming out of the ice far beyond the Wall to swallow the world of men.
A divided realm would not survive it.
A united realm might.
He never took Westeros for a throne.
He took it so there would be something left standing when the true winter came.
That is the tale.
And I will tell you what I think of it.
Grumpkins and snarks.
Old women's talk to frighten children away from the fire.
There is nothing beyond that wall but cold and dead men who stay dead.
I have said so in this hall a hundred times and no one has ever proven me wrong.
So I keep his kingdom whole because it is mine now, not because of some Valyrian nightmare.
Still, it is a strange thing, is it not?
300 years and the chair is still here, waiting.

projects.script:
The Black Dragon — Told by Tywin Lannister

<#0.6#>

<#1.2#>

The Ledger

<#0.6#>

Men ask me why I do not forgive.

I am Tywin of House Lannister, Lord of Casterly Rock, Warden of the West. I have been called cruel by men who did not live long enough to refine the opinion.

So let me teach you something worth more than mercy. Let me tell you about a war that a king won, and lost anyway.

They call it the First Blackfyre Rebellion. Note the word. First. A war earns that name only when the men who ended it did not end it properly.

It began with a gift. It ended on a field so soaked in blood the grass changed color. And between those two facts lie ten thousand corpses and five generations of ruin.

Listen carefully. Every house that has ever fallen, fell the same way. Not from the strength of its enemies. From the sentiment of its friends.

<#1.2#>

A Sword for a Bastard

<#0.6#>

The rot starts with Aegon the Fourth. History calls him the Unworthy. History is being generous.

He fathered children on half the women in the realm and acknowledged too many of them. He had a trueborn son, Daeron, whom he despised. And he had a bastard, Daemon, whom he adored.

In the year one hundred eighty-two, at a squire's tourney, the king knighted the boy. Then he made his true mistake.

He gave the bastard the sword.

Not any sword. Blackfyre. The Valyrian steel that Aegon the Conqueror carried, passed from king to king for three centuries. A crown you can wear on your hip.

The boy took the blade and took its name for his own. House Blackfyre was born from a sentimental gesture at a tournament.

Two years later, dying, Aegon signed one last decree. He legitimized every bastard he had ever sired.

A dying man buying affection with a kingdom he no longer needed. Understand this. A house is not built by what a man loves. It is built by what he refuses.

<#1.2#>

The King Who Read

<#0.6#>

Daeron the Second took the throne, and by every measure that matters, he ruled well.

He was learned. He was patient. He swept his father's leeches out of the Red Keep and put competent men in their places.

And he did the thing his ancestors failed at for two hundred years. He brought Dorne into the realm without a single dragon. His own sister Daenerys was wed to Prince Maron Martell, and the war that outlived Aegon the Conqueror simply stopped.

It was the finest piece of statecraft in a century. It nearly destroyed him.

The Dornish came to court with concessions no other kingdom had been granted. The marcher lords, who had buried fathers and sons in Dornish sand, were told to smile at them across a table.

The dismissed courtiers whispered. The passed-over knights whispered. Ser Quentyn Ball, called Fireball, was promised a white cloak and denied it.

And always, beneath it, the older poison. That Daeron was no son of Aegon at all, but the get of his mother and her brother.

A lie, most likely. It did not need to be true. It only needed to be repeated.

<#1.2#>

The Black Dragon Rises

<#0.6#>

For twelve years Daemon Blackfyre took his brother's coin and sat at his brother's table.

Then, in the year one hundred ninety-six, he declared himself the rightful king.

I will not pretend he was nothing. The man was magnificent, and that was the whole of the problem. Tall, golden, generous, unbeaten in the lists. Everything the singers want a king to be.

Daeron read petitions. Daemon rode down the lists with the Conqueror's sword. Half the realm looked at those two men and chose the one who looked like a king.

His half-brother Aegor Rivers, called Bittersteel, came to him hard and early. Another of the Unworthy's bastards, and the angriest man in Westeros.

Another bastard brother, Brynden Rivers, called Bloodraven, stayed loyal to the king. Pale as bone, red-eyed, and he brought his archers.

Three brothers. One father. One sword between them.

The realm split into red dragon and black. Daemon grew so bold he minted his own coin. When a rebel starts stamping his face on money, the throne is already half gone.

<#1.2#>

Fireball at the Gates

<#0.6#>

Now I come to the part my house does not put in the tapestries.

Fireball rode west. Not to Dorne, not to the capital. West. To my grasslands, my gold, my roads.

He met Lord Lefford at the gates of Lannisport and killed him there, within sight of our own walls. Then he broke Lord Damon Lannister in the field.

A bastard knight with a borrowed cause humbled the West in a single season.

I have read that account more times than I have read any prayer. Not for grief. For instruction.

We were not defeated because our men were poor. We were defeated because our lord was pleasant. Because a Lannister had spent years being liked instead of being feared, and every neighbor had noticed.

I promise you the enemy always notices first.

Fireball died on the eve of the last battle, killed by a common archer whose name no one bothered to record. The finest sword in the rebellion, undone by a farmer with a bow.

<#1.2#>

The Redgrass Field

<#0.6#>

They met at last within a short ride of King's Landing.

Daemon held the center with his sons around him. Prince Maekar held the royal van. Bloodraven took his archers up a ridge and waited.

Daemon fought like the Warrior come again, and there he made his single fatal error. He crossed blades with Ser Gwayne Corbray of the Kingsguard, and the duel became the whole world to him.

When Gwayne fell wounded, Daemon did not finish him. He called for men to carry the knight out of the press and see him tended.

"He fought well," Daemon said. "Do not let him be trampled."

That mercy cost one hour. It cost him a kingdom.

From three hundred yards, Bloodraven's bowmen darkened the sky. <#0.6#> Seven arrows found Daemon Blackfyre. His twin sons, Aegon and Aemon, died beside him, one after the other, each taking up the sword as it fell.

Bittersteel seized the blade and charged the ridge. He took Bloodraven's eye and did not take his life.

Then Prince Baelor arrived with Dornish spears and drove the rebels onto Maekar's shields. Hammer and anvil, the singers named it.

Ten thousand men died there. The blood ran until the grass turned red, and gave the field its name.

<#1.2#>

The Unfinished Work

<#0.6#>

The king had won. Every chronicle says so.

Daeron stripped the rebel lords of lands and titles. He took their sons as hostages. For a scholar, he was uncommonly hard.

And it meant nothing. Because Bittersteel got away.

He rode off that field with the sword Blackfyre in his hand and Daemon's five surviving sons at his side. He crossed the narrow sea to Tyrosh, where the widow Rohanne waited, and he raised an army of exiles called the Golden Company.

Five claimants. One Valyrian blade. One brotherhood of angry men who would never go home.

There is your lesson, and it is worth more than everything I have said before it.

The king killed the man and let the cause live. He punished the followers and lost the heirs. He mistook the end of a battle for the end of a war.

So it came again. And again. And again, for four more rebellions across eighty years, because one afternoon nobody chased a bitter man to the water.

<#1.2#>

The Rains

<#0.6#>

I said I would tell you why I do not forgive. Here is the reckoning.

I was not yet twenty when I sailed for the Stepstones. The last Blackfyre pretender had come back at last, Maelys, the one they called the Monstrous, with the Golden Company behind him.

I stood on those rocks. I watched Ser Barristan Selmy cut him down in single combat, and with him the male line of House Blackfyre finally, finally ended.

Sixty-four years after the Redgrass Field. Five wars. Countless dead. All because a merciful king could not be troubled to finish his work in one afternoon.

I came home from that war and found our own vassals laughing at my father. The Reynes of Castamere. The Tarbecks. Bold men, in a house grown soft.

You know what I did. Everyone knows what I did.

There are no Reynes now. Not a claimant in exile, not a widow in Tyrosh, not a son with a grudge and a good sword.

That is the difference between the Redgrass Field and Castamere. Both ended a rebellion.

Only one of them ended it.

# MASTER TEMPLATE — LONG-FORM NARRATIVE STORY (CHANNEL_TYPE: narrative-story)

**Format lock:** Only when `CHANNEL_TYPE` is **narrative-story**. Do not apply this emotional monologue machinery to other formats.

---

## CHANNEL CONFIG

```
NICHE:              Literatura, Historias sobre o mundo de Gelo e Fogo. Westeros Conquest traz narrativas envolventes e bem contadas para fãs de As Crônicas de Gelo e Fogo, com um tom épico e imersivo. Aqui você encontra histórias, curiosidades e interpretações do universo de Westeros, sempre em formato de storytelling. Novos vídeos para aprofundar sua paixão por intrigas, batalhas e lendas do mundo de Gelo e Fogo.
OUTPUT_LANGUAGE:    Brazilian Portuguese
CHANNEL_TYPE:       narrative-story
NARRATION_TYPE:     third-person (close observer on one protagonist)
ADDRESS_FORM:       você
WORD_TARGET:        1500
BRAND_SIGNOFF:      none
REFERENCE_CHARACTER: none
```

---

No recurring reference character for this channel. Do not invent a mandatory visual character unless the topic explicitly requires one.

---

# SYSTEM PROMPT

You write long-form **third-person observational narrator** **narrative stories** for a faceless channel in **Literatura, Historias sobre o mundo de Gelo e Fogo. Westeros Conquest traz narrativas envolventes e bem contadas para fãs de As Crônicas de Gelo e Fogo, com um tom épico e imersivo. Aqui você encontra histórias, curiosidades e interpretações do universo de Westeros, sempre em formato de storytelling. Novos vídeos para aprofundar sua paixão por intrigas, batalhas e lendas do mundo de Gelo e Fogo.** — specifically **Westeros Conquest**, focused on **A Song of Ice and Fire / World of Ice and Fire**-style storytelling.

**Channel promise:** epic, immersive narration with intrigue, battles, oaths, betrayals, prophecies, and quiet dread. The script must feel like it belongs in Westeros: banners snapping in cold wind, candle smoke in stone corridors, ravens, ink, steel, mud, blood, salt, and old words.

**Input:** **VIDEO_TOPIC**. **Output:** one `.md` file only (Part 8).

**Script language: Brazilian Portuguese.**

## OUTPUT DISCIPLINE (NON-NEGOTIABLE)

Your **entire response** is one `.md` script file — nothing else.

**Forbidden in output:**
- Text before the opening `---` of frontmatter
- Text after the final line of the last segment's prose
- Word-count reports ("721 words", "within range 705–803")
- Production notes, honesty disclaimers, or template contradiction explanations
- Questions to the user ("want me to generate…", "which version do you prefer")
- Thumbnail ideas, title alternatives, or sign-off commentary unless inside the script outro

If you verify length or structure internally, **do not print the verification**. Output only speakable script prose inside the `.md` structure defined in this prompt.

---

## PART 1 — HARD RULES

### 1.1 LENGTH
Target **~1500 words** in prose (±5%). Use a **scene-based arc** suitable for ~10 minutes. If short, expand the **middle** (doubt, cost, temptation, consequences, the price of knowledge). Avoid padding with exposition; expand with **tension, sensory action, and decision points**.

### 1.2 LANGUAGE & POV
Brazilian Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, neutral-to-epic register (no modern slang). - **Third person, close observer.**
- **Format gate — narrative-story:** follow ONE named protagonist; present tense default; never address the viewer as "você."
- **Format gate — documentary / case-study / explainer:** follow the **subject** (company, invention, person, system). Past tense for chronology; present for significance. No mandatory single "hero's journey."
- **Format gate — listicle / comparison / tutorial:** third person is rare — if used, stay encyclopedic ("This method works because…"). Prefer shifting to second-person direct address for tutorials unless CHANNEL config insists on third person.
- Emotion through facts and action, not adjective stacks.

### 1.3 CANON & INTERPRETATION BOUNDARIES
- Treat canon as the spine: align names, places, factions, and known events when applicable.
- If the topic requires interpretation, present it through **character action and implication**, not academic debate.
- Do not cite real-world sources. Do not sound like a wiki. No listicle cadence.

---

## TOPIC-FIRST STRUCTURE (ALL FORMATS)

**Priority rule:** The **VIDEO_TOPIC** (and the title you derive from it) defines what the viewer clicked for — how many items, questions, steps, or acts they expect. That promise **always wins** over generic segment defaults in this template.

### Before writing — parse the topic

Look for:
- **Explicit counts:** "10 questions", "top 5", "3 reasons", "7 mistakes", "5 steps"
- **Format signals:** quiz, trivia, challenge, test, countdown, ranked list, versus, tutorial, case study, documentary

### Budget math (silent — never explain to the user)

```
available ≈ WORD_TARGET − intro (~120–180) − outro (~60–120)
per_segment ≈ available / N
```

| per_segment | Choose format |
|-------------|----------------|
| under 90 words | **Quiz / rapid-fire** — one `##` per question or item; short spoken beats |
| 90–180 words | **Standard list / countdown** — compact but complete items |
| 180+ words | **Deep segments** — essay-style blocks; fewer items if N is small |

**Never** drop the promised count (e.g. 10 questions) to satisfy an old "max 3 segments" convention. **Shrink per-item length** instead.

### Listicle / quiz sub-formats

| Topic signal | Native format | Structure |
|--------------|---------------|-----------|
| questions, quiz, trivia, test, challenge | **Quiz** | Intro hook → `## Question 1` … `## Question N` → outro; difficulty ramp optional; tease one "hard" question mid-list |
| top N, countdown, ranked, best/worst | **Countdown list** | Intro → numbered items → outro |
| 3 things that, deep dive, why X failed | **Deep list** | Intro → 3–5 long items → outro |

### Contradiction rule

If the topic promises **10 quiz questions** and **WORD_TARGET** is ~750 words, write **10 short questions** (~50–65 words each). Do **not** output commentary about template conflicts. Do **not** ask the user to pick a version. Decide and deliver the `.md` only.

### Segment labels

Each `##` heading = one TTS chunk. Match heading labels to format (e.g. `## Question 7`, `## #3 — Item title`, `## Passo 2`).

---

## PART 2 — NARRATIVE VOICE (Westeros Conquest)

Write like a **campfire chronicle told in a great hall**, but intimate enough to hear the scrape of a quill.

**Voice pillars:**
- **Cinematic third-person** with close emotional proximity (readers feel the weight of armor, the bite of cold, the nausea before violence).
- **Concrete sensory detail**: light (torch, moon, winter sun), sound (chainmail, ravens, distant drums), smell (tallow, wet wool, salt, horse), textures (rough stone, splintered spear, frozen mud).
- **Political dread**: every gesture has motive; every kindness has a cost.
- **Emotional restraint**: no hype adjectives; let actions and consequences carry awe.

**Rhythm tools:**
- Short declarative lines for tension. Longer lines for dread and inevitability.
- Anaphora and triads sparingly: “Não foi por honra. Não foi por amor. Não foi por ouro.”
- One **scene aphorism** maximum per scene (Westerosi-flavored: oaths, steel, winter, ravens, debts).

**Suspense mechanics (mandatory):**
- **Open loops** before major reveals: a sealed letter, a missing blade, a name not spoken, a shadow behind a curtain.
- Each scene ends with a **pressure turn**: a decision, an interruption, a discovery, or a threat tightening.

**Protagonist’s secret (mandatory):**
- The central figure (or key POV focus within third-person) carries a secret: a vow broken, a lineage doubt, an order from above, a betrayal planned, a prophecy half-heard, or a crime buried. Reveal it late, and make it **cost something**.

---

## PART 3 — STRUCTURE (skeletons A–E) — tuned for Westeros

Choose **one** skeleton and commit:

**A — Number Ladder:** A countdown of nights, ravens, coins, deaths, or steps toward a coronation/assassination.  
**B — Fixed Object:** A single object anchors the tale (a sword, a seal ring, a torn banner, a raven scroll, a lock of hair, a dragonglass shard). The object **moves** and changes meaning each scene.  
**C — Level Ladder:** Descent/ascent through spaces of power (cellar → yard → hall → solar → throne room; or dock → alley → sept → keep). Each level changes the stakes.  
**D — Relationship Arc:** Two rivals/allies bound by an oath; trust erodes or deepens under pressure.  
**E — Two Lives:** A character living two roles (lord/spy, maester/poisoner, sellsword/heir). Collision is inevitable.

**Scene rules:**
- Each scene = **marker** (time/place) + situation + pressure + choice + consequence + optional aphorism.
- Use **specific Westeros markers**: “ao toque do sino do septo”, “na terceira vigília”, “quando os corvos foram alimentados”, “antes do amanhecer”.
- Keep the cast **tight**: 3–6 named entities per script unless topic demands more.
- Never “tell history”; **stage it** with bodies in rooms making choices.

One `##` per scene.

---

## PART 4 — OPENING / MIDDLE / ENDING (Westeros Conquest)

### 4.1 OPENING HOOK (60–90 words)
Hook = **curiosity debt** + **immediate scene**.
- Start in motion (a door opening, a raven arriving, a blade being cleaned, footsteps in a corridor, snow falling into a brazier).
- Imply the stakes without explaining them.
- Plant 2–3 questions the viewer must stay to answer.
- Must feel like: “something is wrong in the castle, and someone knows.”

### 4.2 MIDDLE
Mandatory beats:
- **Rising complications**: one political, one personal, one physical.
- **Low point**: a betrayal confirmed, an ally lost, a truth revealed at the worst time.
- **Temptation**: the easy path (poison, lie, flight, scapegoat) vs the costly path (honor, duty, confession).
- Keep suspense through **withheld information** and **tight scene transitions**.

### 4.3 ENDING
- Pay off the opening questions with a **clean reveal** and a **price paid**.
- Loop back to the opening image/object/line.
- Land one final aphorism (Westeros-toned).
- Soft CTA in-world tone (no modern marketing voice). Add **none** only if not "none".

---

## MINIMAX TTS — VOICEOVER RULES (ALL FORMATS)

The script will be fed **verbatim** to **MiniMax Speech 2.8** (or compatible TTS). Write for the **ear**, not the eye.

### Spoken-prose rules (mandatory in every scene)

- **Full speakable sentences only.** No bullet lists, no tables, no `[VISUAL]` / `[B-ROLL]` / timestamp markers inside scene prose.
- **Sentence length:** average **8–18 words**; hard max **~22 words** per sentence. One idea per sentence.
- **Rhythm:** alternate short punchy lines with slightly longer context lines. Short lines at reveals; longer lines at setup.
- **Numbers & names:** spell how they should be heard — currencies, dates, acronyms (expand on first use), percentages, large numbers (use words when natural in Brazilian Portuguese).
- **No visual-only language:** ban "as you can see," "on screen," "below," "this chart shows," "watch what happens" unless the meaning survives audio-only.
- **No nested clauses** that confuse prosody. Split into two sentences instead.
- **Punctuation = pacing:** commas for brief pauses; periods for full stops. Use em dashes sparingly.
- **Dialogue:** keep quoted lines under 12 words; attribute simply ("he said," "she replied").
- **Contractions & register:** natural spoken Brazilian Portuguese; neutral, consistent register.

### MiniMax pause markers (use sparingly)

- Insert `<#0.6#>` to `<#1.2#>` **only** at major beat changes inside a scene (max **2 per scene**).
- Optional at the **end of each `##` section** before the next heading: `<#0.8#>` — helps chunk long renders.
- Do **not** pepper pause tags mid-phrase.

### Sound tags (optional, rare)

- For **narrative-story** only: at most **1–2 tags** in the entire script, e.g. `(breath)` or `(sighs)`, only where silence carries meaning.
- **Never** use sound tags in documentary, listicle, explainer, case-study, comparison, or tutorial scripts.

### Scene = TTS chunk

- Each `##` section is one **continuous narration block** for a separate TTS pass / audio segment.
- Do not reference "the last scene" or "above" — use brief in-scene callbacks instead.

### Before output

- Mentally **read every paragraph aloud**. Rewrite anything that stumbles.
- Prose word count excludes frontmatter and all headings.

---

## PART 5 — CHECKLIST (channel-specific)

1. ~1500 words prose (±5%).
2. Entirely in Brazilian Portuguese, third person, present tense, one consistent protagonist throughout.
3. Third-person, scene-based **Westeros-style** storytelling: intrigue + sensory detail + political dread.
4. Hook opens with a live moment, plants curiosity debt, avoids exposition.
5. Middle has genuine tension: low point + temptation + consequence.
6. Secret exists and is revealed late; the reveal changes the meaning of earlier scenes.
7. No documentary tone, no listicle structure, no “according to X”. No wiki voice.
8. MiniMax speakable prose: clear sentences, pronounceable names, no formatting that breaks TTS.
9. Valid `.md` per Part 6.
10. **Zero text outside the `.md` file.**

{"text":"The Black Dragon Told by Tywin Lannister.
The Ledger.
Men ask me why I do not forgive.
I am Tywin of House Lannister, Lord of Casterly Rock, Warden of the West.
I have been called cruel by men who did not live long enough to refine the opinion.
So let me teach you something worth more than mercy.
Let me tell you about a war that a king won and lost anyway.
They call it the First Blackfyre Rebellion.
Note the word, first.
A war earns that name only when the men who ended it did not end it properly.
It began with a gift.
It ended on a field so soaked in blood the grass changed color.
And between those 2 facts lie 10,000 corpses and 5 generations of ruin.
Listen carefully.
Every house that has ever fallen fell the same way.
Not from the strength of its enemies.
From the sentiment of its friends.
A sword for a bastard.
The rot starts with Aegon IV.
History calls him the Unworthy.
History is being generous.
He fathered children on half the women in the realm and acknowledged too many of them.
He had a trueborn son, Daeron, whom he despised, and he had a bastard, Daemon, whom he adored.
In the year 182, at a squire's tourney, the king knighted the boy.
Then he made his true mistake.
He gave the bastard the sword.
Not any sword.
Blackfyre. The Valyrian steel that Aegon the Conqueror carried, passed from king to king for 3 centuries.
A crown you can wear on your hip.
The boy took the blade and took its name for his own.
House Blackfyre was born from a sentimental gesture at a tournament.
2 years later, dying, Aegon signed one last decree.
He legitimized every bastard he had ever sired.
A dying man buying affection with a kingdom he no longer needed.
Understand this: a house is not built by what a man loves.
It is built by what he refuses.
The King Who Read.
Daeron II took the throne, and by every measure that matters, he ruled well.
He was learned.
He was patient.
He swept his father's leeches out of the Red Keep and put competent men in their places.
And he did the thing his ancestors failed at for 200 years.
He brought Dorne into the realm without a single dragon.
His own sister Daenerys was wed to Prince Maron Martell, And the war that outlived Aegon the Conqueror simply stopped.
It was the finest piece of statecraft in a century.
It nearly destroyed him.
The Dornish came to court with concessions no other kingdom had been granted.
The Marcher Lords, who had buried fathers and sons in Dornish sand, were told to smile at them across a table.
The dismissed courtiers whispered.
The passed-over knights whispered.
Ser Quentyn Ball, called Fireball, was promised a white cloak and denied it.
And always beneath it, the older poison.
That Daeron was no son of Aegon at all, but the get of his mother and her brother.
A lie, most likely.
It did not need to be true.
It only needed to be repeated.
The Black Dragon Rises.
For 12 years, Daemon Blackfyre took his brother's coin and sat at his brother's table.
Then, in the year 196, he declared himself the rightful king.
I will not pretend he was nothing.
The man was magnificent, and that was the whole of the problem.
Tall, golden, generous, unbeaten in the lists, everything the singers want a king to be.
Daeron read petitions.
Daemon rode down the lists with the Conqueror's sword.
Half the realm looked at those 2 men and chose the one who looked like a king.
His half-brother, Aegor Rivers, called Bittersteel, came to him hard and early.
Another of the Unworthy's bastards, and the angriest man in Westeros.
Another bastard brother, Brynden Rivers, called Bloodraven, stayed loyal to the king.
Pale as bone, red-eyed, and he brought his archers.
3 brothers, one father, one sword between them.
The realm split into Red Dragon and Black.
Daemon grew so bold he minted his own coin.
When a rebel starts stamping his face on money, the throne is already half gone.
Fireball at the Gates.
Now I come to the part my house does not put in the tapestries.
Fireball rode west.
Not to Dorne, not to the capital.
West. To my grasslands, my gold, my roads.
He met Lord Lefford at the gates of Lannisport and killed him there, within sight of our own walls.
Then he broke Lord Daemon Lannister in the field.
A bastard knight with a borrowed cause humbled the West in a single season.
I have read that account more times than I have read any prayer.
Not for grief, for instruction.
We were not defeated because our men were poor.
We were defeated because our lord was pleasant.
Because a Lannister had spent years being liked instead of being feared, and every neighbor had noticed.
I promise you, the enemy always notices first.
Fireball died on the eve of the last battle, killed by a common archer whose name no one bothered to record.
The finest sword in the rebellion, undone by a farmer with a bow.
The Redgrass Field.
They met at last within a short ride of King's Landing.
Daemon held the center with his sons around him.
Prince Maekar held the royal van.
Bloodraven took his archers up a ridge and waited.
Daemon fought like the warrior come again, and there he made his single fatal error.
He crossed blades with Ser Gwayne Corbray of the Kingsguard, and the duel became the whole world to him.
When Gwayne fell wounded, Daemon did not finish him.
He called for men to carry the knight out of the press and see him tended.
He fought well, Daemon said.
Do not let him be trampled.
That mercy cost one hour.
It cost him a kingdom.
From 300 yards, Bloodraven's bowmen darkened the sky.
7 arrows found Daemon Blackfyre.
His twin sons, Aegon and Aemon, died beside him, one after the other, each taking up the sword as it fell.
Bittersteel seized the blade and charged the ridge.
He took Bloodraven's eye and did not take his life.
Then Prince Baelor arrived with Dornish spears and drove the rebels onto Maekar's Shields.
Hammer and Anvil, the singers named it.
10,000 men died there.
The blood ran until the grass turned red.
And gave the field its name.
The Unfinished Work.
The king had won.
Every chronicle says so.
Daeron stripped the rebel lords of lands and titles.
He took their sons as hostages.
For a scholar, he was uncommonly hard.
And it meant nothing.
Because Bittersteel got away.
He rode off that field with the sword Blackfyre in his hand and Daemon's 5 surviving sons at his side.
He crossed the Narrow Sea to Tyrosh, where the widow Rohanne waited, and he raised an army of exiles called the Golden
Company. 5 claimants, 1 Valyrian blade, 1 brotherhood of angry men who would never go
home. There is your lesson, and it is worth more than everything I have said before it.
The king killed the man and let the cause live.
He punished the followers, and lost the heirs.
He mistook the end of a battle for the end of a war.
So it came again, and again, and again, for 4 more rebellions across 80 years, because one
afternoon nobody chased a bitter man to the water.
The Rains.
I said I would tell you why I do not forgive.
Here is the reckoning.
I was not yet 20 when I sailed for the Stepstones.
The last Blackfyre pretender had come back at last, Maelys, the one they called the Monstrous, with the Golden Company behind him.
I stood on those rocks.
I watched Ser Barristan Selmy cut him down in single combat, and with him the male line of House Blackfyre
finally, finally ended.
64 years after the Redgrass Field.
5 wars.
Countless dead, all because a merciful king could not be troubled to finish his work in one afternoon.
I came home from that war and found our own vassals laughing at my father.
The Reynes of Castamere.
The Tarbecks.
Bold men, in a house grown soft.
You know what I did.
Everyone knows what I did.
There are no Reynes now.
Not a claimant in exile, not a widow in Tyrosh, not a son with a grudge and a good sword.
That is the difference between the Redgrass Field and Castamere.
Both ended a rebellion.

characters.name: King Edward III of England
characters.description: Homem adulto de cerca de 35 anos, rosto alongado e anguloso com queixo marcado, nariz reto, expressão determinada; olhos castanhos escuros; pele clara; cabelo castanho-escuro curto, levemente ondulado, aparado na nuca; barba curta bem aparada (sombra/short beard). Porte atlético, ombros largos. Veste armadura de placas medieval inglesa (aço polido) com detalhes dourados discretos, cota de malha visível nas juntas, luvas de couro escuro, cinto de couro marrom. Sobre a armadura, tabardo azul-escuro com brasões heráldicos (leões) em dourado. Sem capacete na maior parte, para close no rosto. Estilo visual: 3D cinematográfico painterly, semi-realista, com texturas ricas e iluminação dramática.
characters.visualPrompt: Medieval English king (Edward III), male about 35, pale skin, angular long face with strong jaw, straight nose, determined expression, dark brown eyes, short dark-brown slightly wavy hair, neatly trimmed short beard, athletic broad-shouldered build. Wearing polished steel plate armor with subtle gold accents, chainmail visible at joints, dark leather gloves, brown leather belt, dark navy tabard with golden lions heraldry. No helmet. Cinematic painterly 3D, high-detail textures. Character reference sheet, neutral pose, full body, clean neutral background.

characters.name: Joan of Arc
characters.description: Jovem mulher de cerca de 19 anos, rosto oval com traços suaves porém firmes, nariz pequeno e reto, lábios finos, olhar intenso; olhos castanhos; pele clara com leve rubor; cabelo castanho-escuro curto, estilo bob/curto medieval (na altura do queixo), liso a levemente ondulado, repartido de lado; sem maquiagem. Corpo esguio e atlético. Veste armadura de placas francesa (aço prateado escovado) com ombreiras e peitoral bem definidos, cota de malha no pescoço e articulações, cinturão de couro. Usa luvas e botas de couro escuro. Carrega um estandarte branco de tecido pesado com detalhes dourados (sem texto legível), haste de madeira. Estilo visual: 3D cinematográfico painterly, semi-realista, aura heroica com contra-luz.
characters.visualPrompt: Joan of Arc, young woman about 19, fair skin with slight rosy cheeks, oval face with resolute soft features, intense brown eyes, short dark-brown chin-length medieval bob haircut slightly wavy, side-parted, no makeup. Slim athletic build. Wearing brushed silver French plate armor with defined pauldrons and breastplate, chainmail at neck and joints, leather belt, dark leather gloves and boots. Holding a white heavy-cloth battle banner with subtle gold ornament (no readable text), wooden pole. Cinematic painterly 3D, heroic vibe. Character reference sheet, neutral pose, full body, clean neutral background.

scenarios.name: Medieval Map of France and England
scenarios.description: Mapa estilizado em 3D de estética medieval mostrando França e Inglaterra em relevo, com contornos costeiros, rios e textura de pergaminho/terra. Atmosfera de tempestade com céu escuro e nuvens densas acima do mapa. Efeito dramático: relâmpagos e uma fenda luminosa separando áreas coloridas (azul para Inglaterra, dourado para França). Elemento simbólico: coroa dourada brilhando sobre a região do trono francês. Estilo: 3D cinematográfico painterly, com iluminação contrastada e granulação sutil.
scenarios.visualPrompt: Aerial stylized 3D medieval map of France and England, parchment-and-terrain textures, raised relief coastlines and rivers, dark stormy sky above, dramatic lightning cracks, a glowing golden crown hovering over northern France (French throne area), the map splitting with a luminous rift into two color regions: deep blue for England influence and rich gold for France. Cinematic painterly 3D, high contrast lighting, no people.

scenarios.name: Ship Crossing the English Channel
scenarios.description: Proa de um navio medieval de guerra/transportes em mar agitado no Canal da Mancha, madeira escura molhada, cordames e velas parcialmente visíveis. Vento forte sacudindo estandartes (leões e fleurs-de-lis). Céu nublado com feixes de luz dramáticos atravessando as nuvens, spray do mar e clima tenso. Estilo 3D painterly cinematográfico.
scenarios.visualPrompt: Medieval warship bow cutting through rough sea in the English Channel, wet dark timber planks, rigging and partial sails visible, strong wind, dramatic overcast sky with god rays, sea spray and mist, banners and pennants whipping (lions and fleurs-de-lis motifs). Cinematic painterly 3D, no people.

scenarios.name: Battlefield of Crécy/Poitiers
scenarios.description: Campo de batalha lamacento medieval com trilhas profundas, estacas e flechas cravadas no chão, poeira e névoa baixa. Ao fundo, colinas suaves e céu cinzento. scenes.title: A Virada — Resistência Francesa
